lead: Machine learning builds programs that get better at a job as they see more data. Instead of writing every rule by hand, you give the program examples and let it find the rule. A spam filter that learns from emails you have already marked, a bank that scores a UPI payment for fraud, a site that recommends the next product — all work this way. This chapter gives the standard definition, the terms that go with it, the steps of a machine learning project, and the places the idea is used.
prereq: You need only school-level algebra and the idea of a fraction; probability enters in 1.5.

blocks.text: Machine learning is the study of computer programs whose performance on a task improves with experience. The experience is usually data. A widely used definition makes the three parts explicit.
A program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P if its performance on T, measured by P, improves with E.

blocks.where: T is the task, the job to be done; P is the performance measure, a number that scores how well T is done; E is the experience, usually a set of past examples with known answers. The arrow ↑ means increases.

blocks.text: An example with a known answer is a labelled example, and the answer itself is the label. For a spam filter the label is spam or not spam. The things you measure about an example are its features: word counts, message length, number of links. One example written as a list of feature values is a feature vector.

The model is what gets learned. It is a rule, a set of weights or a formula that turns a feature vector into a prediction. Any single candidate model is called a hypothesis, and the set of all hypotheses the learner may return is the hypothesis space.

Using data is not the same as learning from it. A bank can write a fixed rule by hand — flag any payment above ₹2,00,000 — and that rule uses data but never changes. It is not machine learning. Learning needs a program that adjusts itself when it sees more examples.
Building a machine learning system is a pipeline. Each step feeds the next, and a mistake early on is hard to repair later.

items: Collect data. Gather examples that look like the cases the system will meet in use, and record the labels if the task has them.
Prepare features. Clean the data, drop duplicates, and turn each example into a feature vector of numbers. Scaling features to a common range often helps.
Choose a model. Pick a family of hypotheses that suits the task and the amount of data you have.
Train. Run the learning algorithm on the training set; it searches the hypothesis space and returns the model that scores best.
Evaluate. Measure performance on a separate test set the learner has never seen.
Deploy. Put the model into service and keep watching its performance as real data arrives.

blocks.text: The split into training set and test set carries the whole idea of evaluation. The training set is the experience E. The test set stands in for the future and must never be used to fit the model. Training accuracy alone is misleading, because any model can memorise the examples it was shown.

blocks.where: correct is the number of test examples labelled correctly; total is the number of test examples. The result lies between 0 and 1, and is often written as a percentage.

blocks.text: Machine learning earns its place when the rule is too complex or too changeable to write by hand.

items: Spam filtering. A filter learns from emails already marked spam or not spam, using word counts and sender details as features.

UPI and card fraud. A bank scores each transaction for the chance that it is fraudulent, from amount, time of day, device and distance from the last transaction. Fraud patterns shift, so a model retrained on fresh data beats a fixed rule.
Product recommendation. A shopping site predicts what you will click or buy, from your past clicks, past purchases and the behaviour of similar users.
Crop-yield prediction. Rainfall, soil type, area sown and fertiliser use predict yield in quintals per hectare, helping a farmer or a district office plan.
Medical screening. A model reads test values or images and flags patients who need a closer look. A missed case costs far more than a false alarm, so the performance measure must reflect that.
Speech and language. Voice assistants convert speech to text and translation tools move text between languages; both are learned from large paired datasets.

spec.title: From data to prediction
spec.aria: A flow from training emails through feature vectors and a learning algorithm to a model, which also receives a new email and outputs a spam prediction.

examples.question: A spam filter is trained on 1000 emails: 200 spam and 800 not spam. The learned rule marks an email as spam if it contains the word lottery at least twice. On 10 test emails the rule is right on 8. Write down the task T, the performance measure P and the experience E for this system. Then compute the test accuracy as a fraction and as a percentage.
steps: T, the task: read one email and label it spam or not spam. This is a classification task with two classes.
P, the performance measure: the fraction of test emails whose label the rule gets right. That is accuracy.
E, the experience: the 1000 labelled emails, of which 200 are spam and 800 are not spam.
Check the data: 200 + 800 = 1000 emails, so the spam share is 200 ÷ 1000 = 0.20, that is 20%.
Test outcome: 8 correct out of 10 test emails, so correct = 8 and total = 10.
examples.answer: T is labelling an email spam or not spam, P is the fraction labelled correctly, E is the 1000 labelled emails; the test accuracy is 0.8, that is 80%.
examples.check:
correct = 8
total = 10
accuracy = correct / total
print(accuracy)
print(accuracy * 100)
print(200 / 1000)

traps: Calling any program that uses data machine learning. A hand-written rule that never changes is not learning, however much data passes through it.
Swapping the training set and the test set. Training data is the experience E; test data only measures performance and must never be used to fit the model.
Confusing a feature with a label. A word count is a feature; spam or not spam is the label. The label is what you want to predict.
Quoting training accuracy as the model's real performance. A model can score 100% on the training set and still fail on new inputs.
Writing P as a vague phrase such as 'good performance'. The examiner wants a stated measure, for example the fraction of emails labelled correctly.

quiz.q: State the T, P, E definition of machine learning.
quiz.a: A program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P if its performance on T, measured by P, improves with E.

quiz.q: A shop writes a fixed rule: give a discount to any customer who spends more than ₹5,000. Is this machine learning? Give a reason.
quiz.a: No. The rule is written by hand and never changes when new data arrives, so performance does not improve with experience.

quiz.q: A classifier labels 45 of 50 test emails correctly. Compute its accuracy as a fraction and as a percentage.
quiz.a: correct = 45, total = 50. Accuracy = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.9. As a percentage, 0.9 × 100 = 90%.

quiz.q: A fraud dataset has 4,800 normal and 200 fraudulent transactions. What fraction is fraudulent? A model that calls every transaction normal scores what accuracy?
quiz.a: Total = 4800 + 200 = 5000. Fraudulent fraction = 200 ÷ 5000 = 0.04, that is 4%. The all-normal model is right on 4800 of 5000, so accuracy = 4800 ÷ 5000 = 0.96, that is 96%.

quiz.q: A model scores 99% on the training set and 62% on the test set. What has happened, and what is one way to fix it?
quiz.a: The model has memorised the training examples and does not generalise; this is overfitting. Fixes include collecting more training data, using a simpler model, or applying regularisation. See 1.4.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between a feature vector and a label, using an email example.
quiz.a: The feature vector is what you measure about one example: for an email, word counts and message length. The label is the known answer for that example: spam or not spam.

quiz.q: Why must the test set be kept separate from the training set?
quiz.a: Test data stands in for future unseen inputs. If the learner saw it during training, the measured score would be inflated, because the model could reuse those answers instead of learning a general rule.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the pipeline above is usually written as data collection, feature store, training job, evaluation gate and deployment, and the evaluation gate is where most engineering effort goes. The word 'model' now often means a large neural network trained on far more data than a single machine holds; see Unit 5. A model in production can drift as the world changes, so teams monitor accuracy on live traffic and retrain on a schedule. Useful terms to search next: MLOps, data drift, confusion matrix, and the scikit-learn library for the standard Python workflow.
